etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Middle French sympathie, from Late Latin sympathīa (“feeling in common”), from Ancient Greek σῠμπᾰ́θειᾰ (sumpátheia, “fellow feeling”), from σῠμπᾰθής (sumpathḗs, “affected by like feelings; exerting mutual influence, interacting”) +‎ -ῐᾰ (-ia, “-y”, nominal suffix). Equivalent to sym- (“acting or considered together”) +‎ -pathy (“feeling”). Displaced native Old English efnþrōwung (literally “suffering with or together”).

definitions.definition: (in the plural) The formal expression of pity or sorrow for someone else's misfortune.

quote.citation: 2004 September 10, Edward Tverdek, “When Libertarians Go Shopping”, in Chicago Reader‎[1]:
quote.text: While you'll probably have her sympathies if your condominium association wants to preapprove your storm door, you'll need to work harder for her support if your boss at the music megastore demands you grow a goatee to help lend the place some indie cred.

definitions.definition: The ability to share the feelings of another.
A feeling of pity or sorrow for the suffering or distress of another.

quote.citation: 2018, Sergeant first class Greg Stube, Conquer Anything: A Green Beret’s Guide to Building Your A-Team:
quote.text: If you want sympathy you’ll find it in the dictionary between shit and syphilis. Sympathy may pay well in the short term, but if you cash in on sympathy, it will take everything from you in the long run.

definitions.definition: (in the plural) Support in the form of shared feelings or opinions.
Feeling of loyalty; tendency towards, agreement with or approval of an opinion or aim; a favorable attitude.
Inclination to think or feel alike; emotional or intellectual accord; common feeling.
Mutual or parallel susceptibility or a condition brought about by it.
(art) Artistic harmony, as of shape or colour in a painting.
An affinity, association or mutual relationship between people or things such that they are correspondingly affected by any condition.

quote.citation: 1858, William Whewell, History of the Inductive Sciences:
quote.text: He observed, also, the frequent sympathy of volcanic and terremotive action in remote districts of the earth's surface, thus showing how deeply seated must be the cause of these convulsions.

quote.citation: 1936, Rollo Ahmed, The Black Art, London: Long, page 121:
quote.text: A peculiarity of were-animals is the sympathy that exists between their animal form and that of the human with whom it is connected.

quote.citation: 1960 December, “The riding of B.R. coaches”, in Trains Illustrated, page 706:
quote.text: The solution to coach riding defects, at least, seems to require much more co-operative practical experiment by all engineering departments to achieve better sympathy between the vehicle body, its undercarriage and the track on which it rides.

quote.citation: 1997, Chris Horrocks, “The Renaissance Episteme”, in Introducing Foucault, Totem Books; Icon Books, →ISBN, page 67:
quote.text: Sympathy likened anything to anything else in universal attraction, e.g. the fate of men to the course of the planets.
